title: Your fridge doesn't make cold. Here's what it really does
caption: Leaving the fridge open makes your kitchen warmer, not cooler. The reason is a little loop of refrigerant that moves heat out.

lines.text: Leaving your fridge open on a hot day won't cool your kitchen. It makes it warmer.

visual.title: Open fridge on a hot day

lines.text: A fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat from the inside to the outside.
The trick is a liquid called refrigerant, flowing around a sealed loop of pipes.
Inside, it runs through thin coils called the evaporator and boils into a gas, far below freezing.
Boiling soaks up heat, so the warmth from your food flows into those coils.
Then a compressor squeezes the gas, which makes it hotter than your kitchen.
It flows through the coils on the back, the condenser, and dumps that heat into the room.
That's why the back of your fridge feels warm. It's the heat from your food.
Cooled down, the gas turns back into a liquid, squeezes through a tiny tube, and gets ice cold again.
Then the loop starts over. That hum you hear is the compressor switching on and off.
So with the door open, it just moves kitchen heat in a circle, and the motor adds extra heat on top.
Tip: vacuum the dust off those coils now and then, so the heat escapes more easily.
